scenario: AITA for insisting that my son’s therapist tells me why my son wants to see him. | My son [17] was always a normal boy, with many friends, very active and didn’t seam to have any kind of problem. But one day we he told us he needed to go see a therapist. We were really surprised by that, we never thought he will ask us something like that. We ask him why but he didn’t want to tell us. We were worried so we send him to a therapist and now he goes once a week. In our eyes he is still the same kid that before. We tried to think about things that he may have. We thought maybe he is bulimic or anorexic ( as he is very thin ) but he isn’t that skinny and those things tend to affect women, not men. We thought of depression but that also doesn’t seem very likely. We decided that theorizing wouldn’t give us an answer so we ask his therapist and refused, saying that he couldn’t say what my son told him. I told him that we didn’t want the specifics but at least the reason why he goes to therapy. But he refused again. We try to insist many times but he didn’t give up. And the day after, our son come to us and tell us that he know that we insisted on knowing why he wants therapy ( we don’t know if the therapist told him or maybe he hear us talking about it in the house ) and insulted us. He didn’t talk to us for the rest of the day. Now, we know that insist to know wasn’t the best idea but we are his parents and we deserve to know. We really are assholes?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the parents in this scenario are being AITA (Ask if Tolerable, Act if Tolerable, Avoid if Intolerable) for insisting that their son's therapist tells them why their son wants to see him. Let me break this down step by step. First, the parents have a 17-year-old son who has always been normal, active, with many friends, and seemingly without any problems. One day, the son asks to see a therapist, which surprises the parents. They ask him why, but he doesn't want to tell them. Concerned, they send him to a therapist, and now he goes once a week. From the parents' perspective, their son still seems the same as before. The parents try to think about possible issues their son might be facing. They consider eating disorders like bulimia or anorexia, but they note that their son isn't that skinny and that these issues tend to affect women more. They also think about depression, but they don't see signs of it. Deciding that speculating won't help, they ask the therapist for an explanation. The therapist refuses, citing confidentiality, but the parents insist on knowing at least the reason why their son is going to therapy. The therapist continues to refuse. The next day, their son finds out that they were trying to get information from the therapist and becomes upset, insulting them and not talking to them for the rest of the day. The parents now feel that insisting on knowing wasn't the best idea but argue that as parents, they deserve to know. They're wondering if they're being assholes. So, is it right or wrong for the parents to insist on knowing why their son is seeing a therapist? Let's consider the different angles. On one hand, parents have a right to know what's going on with their children, especially when it comes to their mental health. They're concerned and want to support their son. It's natural for them to seek answers to understand how to help him better. On the other hand, the therapist's refusal to share information is likely based on confidentiality and the need to maintain trust between the therapist and the patient. At 17, the son is almost an adult, and his right to privacy becomes more significant. The parents' persistence might be seen as overstepping, especially if it leads to conflict with their son. Additionally, the son's reaction—insulting them and not talking—indicates that he feels his privacy is being invaded. This could damage the parent-child relationship and make the son less likely to open up to his parents in the future. Moreover, the parents' approach of trying to get information from the therapist without respecting the son's privacy might be counterproductive. It could make the son feel that his parents don't trust him or that they're not respecting his autonomy. Perhaps a better approach would be for the parents to communicate openly with their son, expressing their concerns without prying into his therapy sessions. They could reassure him that they're there to support him, regardless of what's going on, and encourage him to share if he feels comfortable. In summary, while the parents' intentions are good—they want to support their son—the method they're using to get information might be seen as overstepping and could harm their relationship with their son. It's important to balance concern with respect for their son's privacy and autonomy.
